A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reward-decomposition and data-prioritization method. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model and induced-policy experiments, including SHP-based bias studies, Reward-Bench evaluations, AlpacaEval-2, MT-Bench, and the appendix PKU-SafeRLHF results.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds RLHFlow-trained evaluations, threshold-sensitivity results, and a constructed multiplicative-reward study in Appendix D.2.

M1.justification: The mutual-information objective, binary-search decomposition, importance-sampling approach, and clustering/EMA prioritization with reinsertion remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 retain the same steps. The new precomputation guidance and multiplicative-reward test do not alter the proposed learning procedure.

E1.justification: Training-data coverage changes substantially: v2 adds RLHFlow preference data and removes the separate PKU-SafeRLHF experiment from v1 Appendix E.1. SHP training, its length-biased and adversarial-prompt variants, UltraFeedback generation prompts, and the Reward-Bench, AlpacaEval-2, and MT-Bench evaluation tasks are retained.

E2.justification: Vanilla BT training and RRM remain the comparison methods for reward-model and induced-policy evaluations. The toy experiments retain ordinary training and the original-data-only control. K-means and Otsu were already reported as tested alternatives in v1; v2 supplies fuller quantitative comparisons.

E3.justification: Additional protocols specify a random 300K-example subset of the 700K RLHFlow dataset, a clustering/EMA sweep with weights 0.8 and 0.9, and constructed multiplicative rewards with Gaussian perturbations. These extend the evaluation settings without reported changes to the retained benchmarks’ backbones, metrics, or DPO/Best-of-N designs.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands robustness analysis beyond the retained length-bias and adversarial-prompt studies. Appendix D.2 tests decomposition on constructed multiplicative rewards, while Appendix E.3/Table 9 quantifies sensitivity to EMA weights and clustering choices, extending v1’s brief statement that K-means and Otsu perform similarly.

E5.justification: v1 gives performance tables without seed counts or uncertainty, although Figure 1 already shows variability across sampled prompts. v2 identifies the main scores as three-seed means and adds mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting in Tables 3–8. This substantially improves uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: New RLHFlow results in v2 Table 2(a) report Ours averages of 0.82/0.75 for 8B/7B, versus RRM’s 0.77/0.70. v1’s PKU-SafeRLHF results, including Ours averages of 0.69/0.66, disappear. Table 9 and Appendix D.2 add sensitivity and qualitative results. Retained SHP, toy, and policy means are unchanged; the RLHFlow scores are not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds an explicit multiplicative reward construction, defining length-dependent prompt-free rewards and noisy prompt-related rewards to examine departures from additivity. The mutual-information objective, Theorems 1–2, and essential proofs remain unchanged. The addition does not establish a general non-additive guarantee.

C1.justification: The central decomposition, prioritization, and generalization contributions remain. However, v2 Section 6 newly asserts that the method can benefit training even when additive decomposition fails; v1 presented additivity only as a limitation requiring future work.

C2.justification: v2 adds a weighted-average explanation for usefulness under non-additivity and identifies position bias as a reason generator reward models are unsuitable for decomposition. It also explains threshold robustness through reinsertion. The removed PKU quality explanation is replaced by discussion attributing lower SHP accuracy to fewer samples and potentially more spurious preferences.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents eight A100 40GB GPUs, approximately 12-hour reward training, comparable resource use for policy training/generation, threshold hyperparameter selection, asset licenses, and RLHFlow dataset access. It adds precomputation guidance and explicitly states that code release is pending. These are additional disclosures, not demonstrated changes to existing implementations.

R1.justification: Ji et al. (2024), cited with the removed PKU-SafeRLHF experiment, disappears from the references. Section 5 also removes the blanket contrast that reward-free methods are restricted to fixed datasets. The remaining literature coverage and claimed distinction from prior reward-modeling methods are largely retained.

P1.justification: The six-section main narrative remains intact, with localized rewrites of the introduction, mutual-information explanation, adversarial-data construction, and related work. Appendix subsections are expanded and reorganized, and v2 adds acknowledgments and a conference checklist alongside front-matter and citation-style edits.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main paper from two columns to one, combines v1 Figures 4–5 into Figure 4(a–b), and consolidates five main tables into two multipart tables. It relocates the SHP table and adds uncertainty tables, a sensitivity table, and a multiplicative-reward plot. Existing plot content is otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: Three-seed uncertainty reporting, quantitative threshold-sensitivity results, and clearer compute disclosures improve the evidence’s assessability and reproducibility. The RLHFlow evaluation adds useful support. These gains are tempered by removing the separate PKU-SafeRLHF validation and supporting the broader non-additive applicability claim only with a constructed example. Overall, v2 offers a limited but clear quality improvement.
